text:
**Recommendation: take a middle path. Move the three shared libraries and their heaviest consumers into one monorepo, keep the remaining repositories where they are, and add automated consumer testing so a library change is validated against its real consumers before it is released.** Do not attempt a full 12-repo consolidation now. The deciding reasons: the pain is concentrated in one dependency edge (library to consumers), not spread across all 12 repos; a full migration is the option most likely to blow the one-sprint limit and the CI budget; and team-owned deploys are easiest to preserve if you only move what has to move.

**Why this fixes the shared-library problem specifically.** Today the failure sequence is: a library change merges, a version is bumped and published, and consumers discover breakage days later when they upgrade. The root cause is that the library's CI never runs consumer code. In a monorepo, a library change and the consumers' adaptation land in one pull request, and CI builds and tests every affected consumer before merge. Breakage is found at review time, by the author who has the context, instead of by a consumer team days later. Two further effects matter. First, consumers inside the monorepo reference the library at the source level (TypeScript workspaces, Go modules with workspace or replace directives), so there is no publish-bump-upgrade lag at all. Second, breaking changes become the author's responsibility to complete, which removes the 'late break' pattern. Consumers that stay outside the monorepo still get published packages, but you add a pre-release gate: the library's CI publishes a release candidate and runs the outside consumers' test suites against it (via a CI trigger or reusable workflow) before the stable version is tagged.

**Which repos move.** Pick the three libraries plus the two or three consumers with the most traffic on them, probably two teams' services. Decide by looking at the last quarter's version bumps and incidents; the repos that generated the late breakages are the ones to move. The other repos stay put and adopt the release-candidate gate. If the gate proves sufficient, you may never need to move them; if not, you migrate them later one at a time, outside any deadline.

**Plan within one sprint of stopped feature work.** The principle is that the migration is mostly background work, with the only true freeze being a short cutover window per moved repo. Week 0 (no freeze): choose tooling and agree conventions. Use Nx or Turborepo for TypeScript and Go workspaces in the same repo, with CODEOWNERS giving each team ownership of its directories. Week 1 (background work by two or three engineers, feature work continues): import repos with history preserved (git subtree or filter-repo), set up path-filtered CI, and run the monorepo in parallel as a shadow of the existing repos without cutting anyone over. Week 2 (the freeze, at most two to three days for the affected teams only, the other teams never stop): archive the old repos as read-only, redirect the consumers' dependency declarations to workspace references, and verify each team can still build and deploy. Weeks 3 and 4 (no freeze): fix stragglers, document the workflow, and add the release-candidate gate for external consumers. Total stopped feature work is roughly 5 to 8 engineer-days per affected team, comfortably under one sprint, and unaffected teams lose nothing. Keep a rollback: the old repos stay archived but restorable for a sprint after cutover.

**Deploy ownership is preserved by design.** A monorepo changes where code lives, not how it ships. Each service keeps its own pipeline, triggered only by changes under its path or in its dependency graph, and its own deploy schedule and approval. Teams deploy independently, with no release train. The one new rule is that a change to a shared library triggers tests for all consumers but does not force any consumer to deploy; consumers pick up the change at their next scheduled deploy. CODEOWNERS means a library change needs approval from the library's owners, and touching another team's service directory needs that team's review.

**CI cost, concretely.** A monorepo can raise the bill if every commit builds everything, so the controls are part of the design, not an afterthought. Use affected-only builds (Nx affected or Turborepo filters) so a change to one service runs only that service and its dependents. Enable remote caching for TypeScript builds and the Go build and test caches, which typically eliminates the majority of repeated work. Run the full consumer suite only for library changes, which are the minority of PRs, and run expensive integration tests on merge or nightly instead of on every push. Cancel superseded runs on the same PR. Before cutover, take a baseline of current CI minutes per month from the existing repos and set a budget alert at, say, 110 percent of it. Expect library PRs to cost more (they now test all consumers) while ordinary service PRs cost the same or less thanks to caching; the net is likely flat to modestly higher, and you should state that to finance as a forecast with the alert as the safeguard, not as a guarantee. The consumer-gate for external repos adds a small cost per library release, not per commit.

**Risks and costs of this recommendation, honestly.** Splitting across two arrangements (a small monorepo plus nine or so standalone repos) is a permanent inconsistency: two workflows to learn, and the external consumers still have a residual propagation delay, only a shorter, tested one. A monorepo needs ownership of its tooling; assign a named owner (about 10 percent of one engineer's time) or the build config will rot. Path-filtered CI can have gaps where a missed dependency edge skips a test that should have run, so review the graph config early. Shared-repo contention (merge queues, a broken main blocking two teams) is real; mitigate with required checks and a merge queue. History import is imperfect, as blame and old PR links are partly lost. And some engineers will resist cross-team visibility of their code.

**Open questions that could change the answer.** If the baseline CI bill is already tight, run the shadow phase longer before cutover. If the late breakages turn out to come from consumers outside the proposed monorepo scope, widen the move or tighten the gate. If the release-candidate gate alone eliminates most late breaks, you could skip the monorepo entirely, so measure it for one release cycle before committing to the import.
